clinicalPearls: Presents as well-demarcated, dusky erythematous to violaceous plaques with a rim of scale, erosions and later hyperkeratosis, characteristically on the dorsa of the feet and lower legs
Lesions are often symmetrical, may be pruritic or painful, and can be mistaken for psoriasis or eczema
It is strongly associated with chronic hepatitis C virus infection and is regarded as a cutaneous marker of it
Zinc deficiency frequently coexists and zinc repletion can lead to marked improvement
It belongs to the family of necrolytic erythemas that includes necrolytic migratory erythema and nutritional deficiency dermatoses
Biopsy shows psoriasiform hyperplasia with upper epidermal pallor, necrosis of keratinocytes and parakeratosis, overlapping with other necrolytic erythemas
Management combines treatment of the underlying hepatitis C with correction of zinc and other nutritional deficiencies
reference.pathophysiology: Necrolytic acral erythema is a necrolytic erythema most consistently linked to chronic hepatitis C virus infection. Its pathogenesis is thought to involve metabolic and nutritional disturbances associated with liver disease, particularly zinc deficiency and abnormalities of amino-acid, albumin and fatty-acid metabolism, which impair epidermal keratinocyte integrity. The nutrient-deprived upper epidermis undergoes necrolysis with the characteristic pallor, vacuolisation and parakeratosis. The frequent response to zinc supplementation supports a central role for micronutrient deficiency in genetically or hepatically susceptible individuals.
additionalInvestigations: Hepatitis C serology and confirmatory viral RNA testing
Liver function tests and assessment of chronic liver disease
Skin biopsy for the necrolytic epidermal pattern
Serum glucagon if necrolytic migratory erythema is a consideration
redFlags: Undiagnosed chronic hepatitis C with progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma
Extensive erosions with secondary bacterial infection
Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for glucagonoma or other cause
reference.prognosis: Lesions can be chronic and refractory to topical therapy alone but often improve substantially with zinc repletion and successful antiviral treatment of hepatitis C; long-term outcome is influenced by the course of the underlying liver disease.
pitfalls: Treating it as recalcitrant psoriasis or eczema without testing for hepatitis C
Not checking or replacing zinc despite its therapeutic value
Confusing it with necrolytic migratory erythema and missing a glucagonoma, or vice versa
Overlooking progression of underlying chronic liver disease
management: Oral zinc supplementation, which frequently produces marked improvement
Antiviral treatment of the underlying chronic hepatitis C with direct-acting antivirals
Correction of associated nutritional deficiencies, including amino acids and albumin
Adjunctive topical corticosteroids, recognising that topical therapy alone is often insufficient
Monitoring and management of the underlying chronic liver disease
Referral to hepatology and dermatology for coordinated care
